              CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF JASON A. HOWTON
                         INDIVIDUAL INTERVENOR (PRO SE)


JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC AND LCRA
 TRANSMISSION SERVICE CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF
CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST SWITCH TO BIG
          HILL SUBSTATION 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT


                                      May 22,2026


I. INTRODUCTION AND PURPOSE
Q. WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF THIS CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?
A. This cross-rebuttal supplements my Direct Testimony (Item No. 3925, filed May 12,
2026) in five respects. First, I demonstrate through two independent natural
experiments in Applicants' own filed data that the F21-E9-G71 Bell County path
produces results identical to F20/F23 on the two criteria Oncor operationally applied.
Second, I present Routes 295 and 296 as alternatives that are superior on the statutory
factors Oncor failed to weight, including terrain-driven cost, ESA exposure, and
community impact. Third, I challenge the reliability of the habitable structure count as a
route comparison metric, using Applicants' own methodology admissions. Fourth, I
respond to the supporting intervenor testimony of Politis and Avery. Fifth, I address the
Scott methodology findings and a cultural resources concern along the F20/F23
corridor.
Q. WHAT IS THE CORE ARGUMENT?
A. The argument operates on two levels. On Oncor's own two operative criteria,
habitable structures and cost, the F21-E9-G71 path is indistinguishable from F20/F23.
On the statutory factors Oncor omitted, community values, historical and aesthetic
values, and environmental integrity, Routes 295 and 296 are substantially superior.
Additionally, the habitable structure count underlying Oncor's analysis is an aerial
photograph exercise that Applicants' own witnesses acknowledge was overinclusive,
not fully ground-truthed, and includes barns, garages, and sheds that are not confirmed
residential structures. The Commission should weigh those counts accordingly.


Il. THE HABITABLE STRUCTURE COUNT IS AN AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH
EXERCISE, NOT A GROUND SURVEY
 Q. HOW WERE HABITABLE STRUCTURES IDENTIFIED FOR THIS PROCEEDING?
A. Applicants' routing consultants Kimley-Horn and Halff identified habitable structures
using GIS spatial analysis of National Agricultural Imagery Program aerial photography
flown in 2024. Three admissions from Applicants' own filings are directly relevant.


   First: To account for photographic interpretation limitations such as shadows, tree
   canopies, and horizontal accuracy of the aerial photography, all habitable structures
   were identified within a measured distance of 520 feet of the alternative route link
   centerlines, not 500 feet as the regulation specifies. The 520-foot buffer was used
   precisely because the aerial photographs could not reliably locate structures at the
   500-foot threshold. (CCN Application, Appendix F, Table 7-5, Note 1.)
   Second: Not all habitable structures were confirmed by personnel on the ground.
   Halff and Kimley-Horn did not have right-of-entry for every property with an identified
   habitable structure. As a result, some structures were verified through field
   observations from publicly accessible right-of-way, while others were identified solely
   from aerial photography. (Applicants' response to RFI, Docket No. 59315, Item Nos.
   3734, 5451.)
   Third: The methodology includes a BGS category (barn, garage, shed) described
   as structures that 'may be occupied on a regular basis.' These are not confirmed
   residential structures. They are structures that aerial photography identified as
   potentially habitable, but their actual occupancy was not verified. (CCN Application,
   Appendix F, Table 7-5, Note 4.)
Q. WHAT IS THE CONSEQUENCE OF THESE METHODOLOGY LIMITATIONS FOR
ROUTE COMPARISON?
A. A count that is acknowledged to be overinclusive, using a broader buffer than the
regulation requires, including unverified structures, and categorizing barns and sheds as
potentially habitable, is not a reliable basis for comparing routes that differ by 19 or 20
structures. Route 895 has 85 aerial-counted structures. Routes 295 and 296 have 104
and 105. The 19-20 structure differential may reflect real residential impact, or it may
reflect differences in the density of barns, garages, seasonal structures, and hunting
camps along those corridors, none of which are confirmed residential occupancies.
Q. IS THERE ANY EMPIRICAL VALIDATION OF WHICH COUNTED STRUCTURES
REPRESENT ACTUAL OCCUPIED RESIDENCES?
A. Yes. The only ground-truth validation of whether an aerial-photography-identified
structure is an actually occupied residence whose resident is affected by the proposed
route is whether that resident responded in this proceeding. Landowner responses and
intervenor filings are not a statutory routing criterion. But they are the only confirmation
in this record that a photographically-identified structure contains a real person whose
daily life, water supply, agricultural operation, or community relationships are disrupted
by the proposed line. Where the aerial count is high and the residential response
validates it, the count is reliable. Where the aerial count is high and the response per
structure is low, the count may be capturing barns, sheds, and seasonal structures
rather than occupied homes.
    The FM 2843 corridor along Links F20 and F23 is an example of a high-count, high-
   response corridor. The residential character of that community is confirmed not by
   the aerial photograph but by the people who live there. Routes 295 and 296 pass
   through a different corridor where the relationship between the aerial count and
   confirmed residential occupancy has not been established to the same degree. The
   Commission should not treat 85 confirmed residential structures along F20/F23 as
   equivalent in weight to 104 aerial-photograph-identified structures of uncertain
   occupancy along an alternative corridor.
Q. DOES THIS ARGUMENT APPLY TO THE NATURAL EXPERIMENT BETWEEN
ROUTES 430 AND 442?
A. Yes, and it reinforces the finding. Routes 430 and 442 both show 80 habitable
structures using this same aerial methodology. They follow identical paths. The only
difference is the Bell County F-segment. The fact that both routes show the same count
confirms that the F20/F23 vs F21/E9/G71 substitution does not change the number of
aerial-counted structures, because the structures on both paths were counted using the
same overinclusive aerial methodology, not through ground verification. The count is a
product of the methodology, not a ground-truthed measurement.


Ill. THE TWO NATURAL EXPERIMENTS: F21-E9-G71 IS EQUIVALENT ON
ONCOR'S APPLIED CRITERIA
Q. WHAT DO THE TWO NATU RAL EXPERIMENTS ESTABLISH?
A. They establish that on both criteria Oncor operationally applied, specifically
habitable structures and cost: the F21-E9-G71 Bell County path produces outcomes
identical to F20/F23.


   Natural Experiment 1, Routes 894 vs. 899: Route 899 shares 37 of 42 links with
   Route 894, differing only in the Bell County F-segment. Route 894 uses F31-F32-
   F20-F23-G72. Route 899 uses F21-E9-G71. Habitable structures: 85 in both. Cost
   differential: $2,013,000 on a $1.68 billion project, or 0.12 percent. Route 899 is 0.3
   miles shorter.
   Natural Experiment 2, Routes 430 vs. 442: Routes 430 and 442 are identical in
   every link except the same Bell County F-segment. Route 430 uses F31-F32-F20-
   F23-G72. Route 442 uses F21-E9-G71. Habitable structures: 80 in both, using the
   same aerial methodology. Costs approximately equal at $1.73 billion, confirmed by
   Brubaker and Associates (Item No. 4332).
Across two independent route configurations, the same F-segment substitution
produces the same result on both of Oncor's operative criteria. The choice of F20/F23
over F21-E9-G71 has no measurable benefit on the only two factors Oncor applied.
Q. WHAT DO THE STATUTORY FACTORS SHOW ACROSS ALL ALTERNATIVES?
 A. The comparison across all primary alternatives is set out in the following table. The
habitable structure row reflects aerial-counted structures as reported by Applicants,
subject to the methodology limitations discussed in Section Il.

 IV. ROUTES 295 AND 296: SUPERIOR ON THE STATUTORY FACTORS ONCOR
OMITTED
Q. WHY ARE ROUTES 295 AND 296 VIABLE PRIMARY ALTERNATIVES?
A. Routes 295 and 296 take a different Bell County path than either Route 894 or
Route 899. After the shared approach through B21-C4-D12-C5-E52-Fl-F31-F32, they
continue through Links F33-F34-F6-F7 into a different southern corridor, bypassing the
Salado community, the FM 2843 corridor, and the Balcones Escarpment terrain. Their
advantages on the three PURA factors Oncor omitted from its operative analysis are
material.
Q. WHAT IS THE ESA AND ENVIRONMENTAL INTEGRITY ADVANTAGE?
A. Routes 295 and 296 have formal ESA habitat exposure of 107 feet, compared to
461 feet for Route 894, a 77 percent reduction. The ESA metric is drawn from USFWS-
mapped habitat databases. As documented in my father Aaron Edward Howton's direct
testimony (Item No. 3988), GCW has been personally observed within 500 feet of Link
F20. His testimony establishes that the FM 2843 corridor contains GCW habitat that
may not be fully captured in the formal mapped metric. If the actual GCW habitat along
F20/F23 is more extensive than the 461 feet formally recorded, the real ESA advantage
of Routes 295 and 296, which avoid the corridor entirely, is greater than the 77 percent
formal reduction already shows.
Q. WHAT IS THE COMMUNITY VALUES ADVANTAGE?
A. PURA Section 37.056(c)(4)(A) requires the Commission to consider community
values. Routes 295 and 296 bypass the Salado community and the FM 2843 corridor
entirely. They do not affect my property, my father's adjacent property, the Cedar Valley
Baptist Church rebuilt after the April 2022 EF-3 tornado, the Trinity Aquifer-dependent
water wells serving the corridor, or the cedar and oak woodland habitat documented in
the Howton family testimony. The community whose values are at stake along F20/F23,
a rural Bell County corridor with 22-year-resident agricultural families, a rebuilt tornado-
damaged church, and an aquifer-only water supply, is entirely avoided by Routes 295
and 296.
Q. WHAT IS THE COST RELIABILITY ADVANTAGE FROM TERRAIN AND TURNS?
A. The FM 2843 corridor and the terrain south of Salado crosses the Balcones Fault
Zone, a series of offset faults documented in the Bradley testimony (Items No. 4445 and
4568) that creates steep Iimestone cliff faces and incised drainage channels. Routes
295 and 296 diverge from Route 894 at Link F32 and proceed through F33-F34 in a
direction that avoids this terrain feature. In Docket 59336, Applicants' witnesses
admitted that the additional cost for helicopter construction versus on-the-ground
assembly is $130,000 to $1.3 million per mile, depending on terrain. If the F20/F23
corridor requires helicopter work due to this terrain while the F33-F34 corridor of Routes
295 and 296 does not, the filed $2 to $3.6 million cost premium for Routes 295 and 296
may be overstated or may not exist when terrain-adjusted construction costs are
properly accounted for.
    Routes 295 and 296 also proceed more directly south through F33-F34 without the
   lateral deviation toward Salado that Links F20 and F23 create. Fewer directional
   changes mean fewer running angle structures, less steel per mile, and less tariff
   exposure on the heavier structure type. Ms. Cooley admitted that cost estimates
   used estimated turning angles by link but did not disclose the turning angle
   assumptions for Route 894 versus Routes 295 and 296 at the F32 junction. That
   question is the subject of RFI-JAH-S5-17 filed in this proceeding. Until answered, the
   terrain and turn-adjusted cost comparison between Route 894 and Routes 295 and
   296 remains unresolved.


V. REBUTTAL OF TESTIMONY SUPPORTING ROUTE 894
Q. HOW DOES THIS ANALYSIS RESPOND TO THE POLITIS AND AVERY
TESTIMONY?
A. Nikolaos Politis (Item No. 3986) testified that Route 894 best meets all routing
criteria, criticizing Routes 295 and 296 as more costly. Mike Avery (Item No. 3987)
offered similar testimony. Neither witness addresses Route 899, which is not more
costly than Route 894 in any meaningful sense. Neither addresses the terrain-adjusted
cost argument for Routes 295 and 296. Neither addresses the GCW ESA advantage of
Routes 295 and 296. And neither engages with the habitable structure methodology
limitations that render the 19-20 structure differential between Route 894 and Routes
295/296 unreliable as presented. The supporting testimony assumed the aerial count is
reliable and complete. It is not.
Q. DOES THE COST COMPARISON IN THE SUPPORTING TESTIMONY REFLECT
CURRENT CONDITIONS?
A. No. Ms. Cooley admitted that cost estimates are based on historical costs not
subject to current tariffs, that tariffs on aluminum, steel, and copper will likely increase
project costs materially, and that Applicants cannot quantify the impact. A cost
comparison built on a historical baseline that all witnesses acknowledge is inaccurate
cannot be the deciding factor between Route 894 and any alternative, particularly when
the filed differential between Route 894 and Routes 295/296 is smaller than any
plausible tariff adjustment on the higher-structure-type miles those routes share with
Route 894.


VI. ALIGNMENT WITH THE SCOTT METHODOLOGY FINDINGS
Q. HOW DOES SCOTT'S TESTIMONY SUPPORT THIS ANALYSIS?
A. Mr. Scott testified (Item No. 4507) that Applicants filed no routing methodology
document, drew the study area post-hoc around predetermined routes, explored
territory 2.6 times smaller than the legitimate statutory area, and produced alternatives
that cluster around a predetermined path at a Centerline Gravity Index of 3.37 percent.
These findings explain how the terrain advantages of Routes 295/296, the ESA
advantage on the F33/F34 corridor, the turning angle cost differential, and the habitable
 structure methodology limitations all went unweighted and undisclosed. A methodology
that applied only two of eleven applicable statutory criteria and was never documented
for the record would not identify these factors.
Q. DO YOU SEEK THE SAME REMEDY AS SCOTT?
A. No. My remedy is narrower: modify the Bell County segment using filed alternatives
already before the Commission. No new analysis is required.


VII. CULTURAL RESOURCES CONCERN
Q. WHAT CONCERN DO YOU RAISE?
A. In my direct testimony I documented my property's location in the Salado Creek
watershed, downstream from the Gault Site, a pre-Clovis site of national significance
with documented occupation approximately 20,000 years before present. I have been
informed by a neighboring Iandowner whose property abuts Link F20 that pre-contact
cultural resource sites may exist on their property. I cannot attest to the existence or
significance of those resources. However, the cultural resources assessment conducted
by Halff and Kimley-Horn was limited to THC-recorded sites, the same overinclusive-
but-unverified approach used for habitable structures. Applicants admitted in response
to Keith Smith RFI No. 2-02 that they cannot confirm whether actual historical sites fall
within 500 feet of any proposed centerline. A corridor with documented pre-Clovis
occupation density in its watershed warrants site-specific archaeological survey before
construction.
Q. WHAT DO YOU REQUEST?
A. If any route through Links F20 or F23 is approved, I request the Commission
condition that approval on a Phase 1 archaeological survey of the Bell County F-
segment before ground-disturbing construction, with results filed in this docket.


Vlll. RECOMMENDED ACTION
Q. WHAT DOES THE EVIDENCE SUPPORT?
A. The record supports approval of a route that avoids Links F20 and F23, chosen from
among the alternatives already filed. Three specific alternatives serve distinct analytical
functions:

   Route 899 (equivalence argument): Shares 37 of 42 links with Route 894.
   Identical habitable structure count. Cost within 0.12 percent. Route 899 is the
   narrowest possible remedy, a single Bell County segment substitution. It proves that
   F20/F23 can be avoided at effectively zero additional cost with no change in the
   structure count metric Oncor applied.
   Routes 295 and 296 (community values and environmental argument): Bypass
   the FM 2843 corridor and Salado community entirely. Reduce formal ESA exposure
    by 77 percent. Avoid the Balcones Escarpment terrain with its helicopter cost
   premium. Require fewer angle structures with lower per-unit tariff exposure. Their
   19-20 additional aerial-counted structures must be weighed against these
   advantages under the five-factor statutory standard, particularly given that the
   habitable structure count methodology was not ground-truthed and includes BGS
   structures of uncertain occupancy.
   Route 442 (habitable structure argument): Uses the F21-E9-G71 path. Avoids
   F20 and F23. Has 80 habitable structures, five fewer than Route 894 on the same
   aerial methodology.

I additionally request that the Commission: (1) require updated cost estimates reflecting
current Section 232 tariff rates and terrain-adjusted construction assumptions before
any procurement commitments are made; and (2) condition any approval of a route
through F20 or F23 on a Phase 1 archaeological survey of the Bell County F-segment
before ground disturbance.
